newsitem.title: USA: White House proposed FY 1998 EPA budget up 12 pct.
newsitem.headline: White House proposed FY 1998 EPA budget up 12 pct.

text.p: The White House Thursday proposed a 12 pct increase in the Environmental Protection Agency's fiscal 1998 budget over 1997.
The White House proposed a $7.645 billion budget, including operating expenses and various funds and loan programs, for next fiscal year, up from $6.799 billion this fiscal year.
Included in that, the White House is seeking $3.4 billion for the agency's operating program, which includes most research, regulation, grants with states and tribes, and enforcement programs.
That would be up nine percent from this fiscal year.
The budget plan would increase state revolving funds for loans on projects to improve water quality to $1.07 billion from fiscal 1997's $625 billion, a 72 percent increase.
But it would reduce state revolving funds for loans on drinking water projects to $725 million from fiscal 1997's $1.275 billion, a 43 percent drop.
The budget proposed spending $2.094 billion on the Superfund hazardous waste clean-up program next fiscal year, up 50 percent from the current $1.394 billion.

The budget document said that is to "begin meeting the President's pledge to nearly double the pace of Superfund cleanups." The EPA proposed cleaning up another 500 sites in the next four years, which would mean about two-thirds of the nation's Superfund sites would be cleaned by 2000.
To ensure available funding, the budget proposed extending Superfund taxes that have expired and would fund clean-up costs attributed to parties that were no longer solvent.
The plan also would provide an additional $75 million to the Brownfields initiative to clean up urban toxic waste sites.
The Brownfields budget plan would boost grants to communities for site assessment and redevelopment planning and to support a revolving loan fund by $50 million to a total of $88 million.
It also would boost by $25 million funding for the Department of Housing and Urban Development to leverage state, local and private funds to redevelop cleaned-up sites.
